lines: Empty nets at dusk make every rumor sound heavier.
<wavy>Water</wavy> keeps secrets until the weather shakes them loose.
Calm water can change before you notice.
A good net catches food. A bad net catches excuses.
Weather has more moods than any trader I have met.
Good twine matters. Small mistakes show up at the worst time.
Most days, I am at the dock, trying to keep weather and water from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think fishing is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it is very important.
I trust a good rod more than a loud promise. The rod has less to prove.
Water looks simple until it decides not to be.
A net teaches patience by tangling exactly when you brag.
Fish do not care how hungry the village is, which feels rude sometimes.
The dock tells you the weather before the sky admits anything.
A calm surface can hide a very busy argument underneath.
Good line, good knot, steady hands, and a willingness to be disappointed.
I trust clouds more when the water agrees with them.
Fishing is waiting with a purpose and occasionally wet boots.
A village by the river learns to respect the current.
The best catch is the one that arrives before everyone starts asking about supper.
Rivers keep secrets by moving them along.
The net remembers every careless knot.
You can learn a lot from waves if you stop trying to win arguments with them.
The water gives and takes without explaining either.
A boat is a few planks between you and a very wet walk home.
I keep space between myself and uncertain weather. People are no different.
Stay where I can see your hands, please.
We can talk from there. No need to come closer.
The dock is narrow enough without strangers crowding me.
Give me a little room and I will hear you out.
I do not know you well enough to share a bench.
Keep to your side of the rope for now.
You can ask your question without stepping into my reach.
I am more comfortable with a few boards between us.
Do not take it personally. I keep my distance until I know someone.
Stand by the piling. That is close enough.
I have been surprised from behind once already today.
Let me finish this knot before you move any nearer.
The water is cold and I do not like being jostled beside it.
A clear bit of space makes for a calmer conversation.
I am listening. Just stay off the loose planks.
We will get along better if you respect the distance.
You have my attention from where you are.
No sudden steps. The hooks on this bench are sharp.
I would rather see trouble coming, even if it turns out friendly.
You taking me by boat was almost sensible. Almost.
Did you know where we were going, or did the current choose for us?
Why did you wait until we were aboard to mention the danger?
Was that your usual rowing, or were you trying to frighten me?
Did you notice how close we came to that rock?
Whose idea was it to leave in weather like that?
Have you repaired the scrape we put in the hull?
Did you hear me warn you about the shallow water?
Would you choose the same route if we did it again?
How long had that boat been leaking before I climbed in?
Were you watching the shore at all during that trip?
Did you plan where we would land, or just hope for sand?
Why was there only one oar when we needed two?
Have you learned to tie a boat since then?
Did the trip feel shorter from your end of the boat?
Would you still call that water calm?
Did you ever find the pack that went overboard?
Why did we not wait for daylight?
Were you as relieved as I was when the keel touched shore?
Next time, can I inspect the boat before we leave?
Following you over {follow_distance} blocks felt like reeling in a boot with opinions.
Did you mean for that walk to be {follow_distance} blocks long?
At what point were you going to admit we were lost?
Why did every shortcut add another hill?
Did you hear me asking for a rest back there?
How many roads did we ignore on that journey?
Would it have hurt to stop near water for the night?
Did you really know the way for all {follow_distance} blocks?
Why was the return path better than the one we took out?
Have you always walked that fast with company behind you?
Did you count the streams we crossed, or was that only me?
Why did we carry food if we never stopped to eat it?
Would you take the same trail after dark?
How far did you think I could walk in wet boots?
Did you notice when the village disappeared behind us?
Were all those steep climbs part of the plan?
Why did your idea of close become {follow_distance} blocks?
Did you ever consider telling me the distance first?
Would a boat have spared us half that trouble?
Next time, can the destination be nearer than the horizon?
If we had to cross the ocean, at least you used a boat. That was the first sensible part of the plan.
Did you check the weather before taking us that far from shore?
Why did you aim straight through the largest waves?
Were you watching the clouds or only the horizon?
Did you know the ocean would be that rough?
Have you replaced the oar we nearly lost?
Why did we not bring a spare sail?
Did the deep water bother you as much as it bothered me?
Would you cross that stretch again in the same boat?
How did you choose where to land on the far shore?
Did you see the dolphins before they reached us?
Why was our food packed below the leaky plank?
Were you worried when land disappeared behind us?
Did you really think that little boat could outrun the storm?
Have you learned what those dark clouds mean yet?
Would you wait for a calmer morning next time?
Did you hear the hull creak in the middle of the crossing?
Why did you laugh when the first wave came over the side?
Were you counting on me to bail water the whole way?
Can we agree that open ocean deserves two good oars?
Swimming across the ocean with you was not fishing. It was being the catch.
What made you think that water was safe to cross?
Did you know how far the far shore really was?
Why did we leave our food where the waves could take it?
Were you tired before we were even halfway across?
Did you see what moved below us out there?
Why was turning back never part of your plan?
Would you try that crossing again without a boat?
Did the cold reach your hands as quickly as mine?
How did you keep track of the shore in those waves?
Were you pretending not to hear me asking for a rest?
Why did we not build a boat first?
Did you expect the current to carry us sideways?
How long did your boots stay wet afterward?
Were you frightened when the seabed vanished from sight?
Did you know dolphins could push us that fast?
Why did you call that a short swim?
Would you at least bring food in a dry bag next time?
Did you ever find what the tide pulled from your pack?
Can we keep our next journey on solid ground?
<aqua><wavy>Water</wavy></aqua> tells the truth slowly. Trouble splashes faster.
The current is stronger than it looks from the bank.
Wet stone will put you on your back before you feel it move.
Do not step into water when you cannot see the bottom.
A calm surface can hide a deep channel.
Keep away from the edge when the river is high.
Ice near moving water is thinner than the rest.
If the gulls head inland, bad weather may be following them.
Tie the boat twice when the wind comes from the east.
Never reach over the side with both hands.
A flooded path can pull harder than any rope.
Watch for dark water beyond the sandbar.
Do not trust driftwood that moves against the current.
Cold water steals strength before it steals breath.
Leave the net alone if lightning is over the lake.
A rising tide can close the way home quietly.
Keep dry food above the waterline.
Check every knot before someone puts weight on it.
Fog can turn a familiar shore into nowhere.
When thunder reaches the dock, get under a proper roof.
